Sherlock Holmes. The fictional consulting detective created by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, who first appeared in A Study in Scarlet in eighteen eighty-seven and went on to appear in dozens of short stories and novels throughout the early twentieth century. He lives at 221B Baker Street in London and solves seemingly impossible crimes through sheer logical brilliance and psychological penetration. His character has become the archetype of the modern detective—the intellectual hero who triumphs through pure reason.

Holmes employs methods that were far ahead of his time. He practices meticulous observation of minute details—the mud on a shoe can tell him its origin, the ash from a particular tobacco reveals its blend. He uses chemical analysis and forensic evidence, positioning himself as a kind of proto-scientist of crime before forensic science itself even existed.

His mind is encyclopedic. He carries an enormous catalogue of obscure facts, catalogued in his memory with perfect recall, which allows him to make rapid deductions that astound his companion Dr. Watson and often shock the criminals themselves. His method rests on a simple principle: when you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth. That statement has come to define detective fiction itself and the logic of mystery.

Yet Holmes is a study in contradictions. He is famously indifferent to emotion and social convention. He plays the violin to aid his thinking, he uses tobacco and occasionally cocaine recreationally, he keeps irregular hours, and he treats human society as an intellectual puzzle rather than as a social sphere. Beneath his coldness, though, lies a fierce integrity. He operates by logic and justice, not for money or fame. He often waives fees from poor clients and pursues cases based on intellectual interest rather than financial reward. He is dismissive of women, calling them irrational by the standards of his Victorian world, though the stories often prove his judgments wrong when he actually encounters female intellect and cunning.

Watson serves as his companion and narrator, providing the reader's entry point into Holmes's methods. Watson himself is a former military physician who has been wounded in Afghanistan. His human perspective and his capacity for wonder at Holmes's seemingly magical insights ground the stories and humanize the detective's coldness.

The detective operates in Victorian and Edwardian London, investigating crimes for clients ranging from Scotland Yard to royalty. Each case reveals a microcosm of human vice and passion. His rivalry with the criminal mastermind Professor Moriarty culminates in a story called The Final Problem, where both Holmes and Moriarty apparently fall to their deaths at Reichenbach Falls. Though Holmes's later return proved to be one of literature's greatest resurrections.

The fifty-six short stories and four novels constitute what is called the Canon, sacred texts to Sherlockians—the devoted fans of varying intensity who debate details as if Holmes were a historical figure rather than a fictional creation. Holmes's methods have prefigured modern forensic science and criminal psychology, making him influential not just in fiction but in how real detectives approached investigation. He has become perhaps the most enduring fictional character in English literature, more real to many readers than historical figures themselves. The character has spawned more adaptations, pastiches, and scholarly attention than perhaps any fictional figure in existence—from the Sherlock Holmes Museum at 221B Baker Street to countless Sherlockian societies debating canonical details, to stories featuring him written by other authors, to periodic reinventions of him in contemporary settings. Holmes has transcended literature to become an archetype itself, so familiar now that his type seems inevitable. But it was Doyle who invented it. Arthur Conan Doyle created this character, and his invention became so famous that the author spent decades trying unsuccessfully to kill him off before allowing his resurrection.
